title: Meta Just Started Cutting 8,000 Jobs. For Thousands of Indian Engineers, the AI Pivot Means a Pink Slip — or a Forced Reassignment.
excerpt: Singapore staff were notified at 4 a.m. The rest of the world followed. Inside Meta's biggest restructuring since 2023 — and why Indian tech workers are disproportionately feeling the blade.
body:
The emails started arriving at 4 a.m. Singapore time on Wednesday. By the time Meta's offices in California opened for business, the company's largest round of layoffs since 2023 was well underway — a global restructuring that will eliminate approximately 8,000 roles and forcibly reassign another 7,000 employees into AI-focused positions.

The cuts amount to roughly 10% of Meta's total workforce and represent the sharpest single reduction since Mark Zuckerberg's "Year of Efficiency" bloodbath in 2023. An additional 6,000 open positions will go unfilled. Staff were encouraged to work from home during what multiple sources described as a "doomsday" atmosphere, with employees reportedly stocking up on free snacks, company-branded chargers, and other perks before losing their access badges.

## The AI Bet Behind the Blade

The restructuring is not an austerity measure in the traditional sense. Meta reported $56 billion in quarterly advertising revenue in its most recent earnings and has guided for capital expenditure of $125 billion to $145 billion in 2026 — a staggering sum directed almost entirely at AI infrastructure. The layoffs are designed to redirect human capital, not merely reduce headcount: Zuckerberg wants fewer managers, flatter hierarchies, and a workforce organised into small, AI-native "pods" that can ship products faster.

An internal document circulated ahead of the cuts laid out the plan in clinical detail. Affected employees would be notified in three waves, staggered by time zone. Engineering and product teams are expected to bear the brunt, with management layers specifically targeted for elimination. Those not laid off but reassigned will be moved into AI-focused teams — in some cases, with explicit instructions to help train the systems that may eventually automate their former roles.

"We're going to make changes to remove layers of management to make decisions faster, invest more in building AI tools that make engineers more productive and move some people to different roles," Zuckerberg wrote in a company-wide note in April. "In a small number of cases, this will mean roles are eliminated."

The language was measured. The scale was not.

## The Indian Dimension

Meta employs thousands of engineers, product managers, and data scientists of Indian origin — both at its Menlo Park headquarters and across offices in Hyderabad, Gurugram, and Singapore. The company's engineering teams have long been among the most coveted destinations for Indian computer science graduates, both through domestic hiring and the H-1B visa pipeline.

For H-1B holders in the United States, a layoff is not merely a career setback. Under current immigration rules, a terminated H-1B worker has a 60-day grace period to find new sponsoring employment or face deportation. In a job market where the tech industry has collectively shed over 110,000 positions in 2026 alone — with Oracle cutting 30,000 jobs, Microsoft offering voluntary buyouts, and LinkedIn trimming over 600 roles on the same day — that 60-day window can feel vanishingly small.

The Indian tech community on social media was lit up within hours of the first notifications. LinkedIn posts from affected employees — some naming Meta directly, others posting cryptically about "exploring new opportunities" — began appearing by Wednesday morning Pacific time. Several Indian-origin former employees described weeks of quiet dread preceding the announcement.

## The Bigger Picture

Meta is not acting alone. Stanford researchers tracking early-career technology and marketing roles for workers aged 22 to 25 found a net 20% headcount reduction attributable to AI automation in 2026. The throughline across the industry is consistent: companies are spending more on AI infrastructure and less on the human beings who used to do the work those systems are now being trained to perform.

For Indian tech workers — who represent a disproportionate share of the engineering talent at virtually every major Silicon Valley firm — the implications are structural. The H-1B system was built for an era of sustained tech hiring. Whether it can survive an era of AI-driven workforce compression is a question that Washington has barely begun to ask.

Zuckerberg has framed the restructuring as a bet on "personal super-intelligence" for Meta's 3.9 billion monthly active users. For the 8,000 people who woke up to termination notices on Wednesday morning, the phrase carries a rather different kind of weight.
